section.title: Set a Guard over My Mouth
section.sectionRationale: A Davidic lament framing prayer itself as incense and evening sacrifice, this psalm turns from crying for rescue outward, Psalm 140, to guarding the heart and mouth within, its welcome of a righteous friend's rebuke as oil for the head modeling the humility that keeps a believer from sliding into the very evil he prays against.
section.thesis: David asks the LORD not only to rescue him from external violence but to guard his own mouth and heart from evil, welcoming a righteous friend's rebuke as kindness while trusting God alone to spring the traps of evildoers, so that he may pass by safely while they fall into their own snares.
section.frameNote: Three movements: a fragrant, urgent cry for God to hear, verses 1-2; the plea for a guarded mouth and heart, including welcome of righteous rebuke, verses 3-7; and eyes fixed on God alone for refuge from hidden snares, verses 8-10.

units.label: Let my prayer be set before You like incense

verses.text: I call upon You, O LORD; come quickly to me. Hear my voice when I call to You.
May my prayer be set before You like {{ketoret|incense}}; my uplifted hands, like the evening offering.

units.label: Set a guard over my mouth

verses.text: Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch at the door of my lips.
Do not let my heart be drawn to any evil thing or take part in works of wickedness with men who do iniquity; let me not feast on their delicacies.
Let the righteous man strike me; let his {{tokhechah|rebuke}} be an act of loving devotion. It is oil for my head; let me not refuse it. For my prayer is ever against the deeds of the wicked.
When their rulers are thrown down from the cliffs, the people will listen to my words, for they are pleasant.
As when one plows and breaks up the soil, so our bones have been scattered at the mouth of Sheol.

units.label: My eyes are fixed on You

verses.text: But my eyes are fixed on You, O GOD the Lord. In You I seek refuge; do not leave my soul defenseless.
Keep me from the snares they have laid for me, and from the lures of evildoers.
Let the wicked fall into their own nets, while I pass by in safety.

ketoret.gloss: Incense, burned morning and evening at the temple, Exodus 30:7-8. David asks that his prayer, offered far from the sanctuary, be received by God with the same acceptance as the fragrant, appointed incense offering.

tokhechah.gloss: Rebuke, correction, reproof. David welcomes the tokhechah of a righteous friend as an act of loving devotion, likening it to healing oil poured on the head, a striking picture of correction received as kindness rather than resented as attack.

basic.context: David prays with the language of temple worship, incense and evening offering, even while apparently far from the sanctuary, asking not only for rescue from enemies but for a guarded mouth and heart, and welcoming the correction of a righteous friend as a kindness rather than an insult.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm describes David's own urgent, worshipful prayer life amid danger from without and temptation from within; it prescribes framing all prayer as an offering to God, guarding one's own speech and heart, and receiving godly rebuke as grace rather than as a burden to be refused.
basic.originalLanguages: David asks that his prayer be received like ketoret, incense, the fragrant offering burned morning and evening at the temple, Exodus 30:7-8. He welcomes a friend's tokhechah, rebuke, as an act of loving devotion, oil for his head, a correction that heals rather than wounds.
basic.typology: David's prayer offered like incense anticipates the saints' prayers pictured as incense before God's throne, Revelation 5:8, and his welcome of righteous rebuke as oil for the head anticipates Christ's own pattern of receiving no deceit and returning no threats under unjust treatment, 1 Peter 2:22-23.
basic.christ: Christ embodies this psalm's guarded mouth perfectly, committing no sin, no deceit found in His mouth, and when reviled, He did not revile in return, 1 Peter 2:22-23, and He now intercedes for His people, presenting their prayers, like this psalm's incense, acceptable before the Father.
basic.god: God is shown as the one who receives prayer as a fragrant offering, who alone can guard mouth and heart from evil, and who is trusted as refuge from every hidden trap, while human correction, rightly received, becomes one of His means of keeping His people from stumbling.
basic.crossReferences: Proverbs 27:6 states the same principle as verse 5, faithful are the wounds of a friend. Revelation 5:8 pictures the saints' prayers as incense before God's throne, echoing verse 2. 1 Peter 2:22-23 shows Christ's own guarded mouth under unjust attack, the fulfillment of David's plea in verse 3.
basic.oneStory: David's prayer offered like incense, his guarded mouth, and his welcome of a friend's healing rebuke anticipate Christ, whose mouth held no deceit and who now presents His people's prayers acceptably before the Father, teaching every believer both how to pray and how to receive correction as grace.

context.literary:
Psalm 141 is a short prayer with a clear arc, and its parts are held together by the body. It speaks of the voice, the hands, the mouth, the lips, the heart, the head, the bones, the eyes and the soul. A reader who follows those parts through the poem sees a person offering his whole self to God and then asking God to guard each part.

The first section, verses 1 and 2, is the call and the offering. It opens with 'I call upon You' and asks that God hear 'my voice when I call to You,' so the voice is the first thing offered. Verse 2 turns the prayer into a ritual picture: it is 'set before You like incense,' and the lifted hands are 'like the evening offering.' The second section, verses 3 and 4, asks for a guard on the mouth and the heart, and the third, verse 5, accepts the rebuke of a righteous friend and refuses the company of the wicked. Verses 6 and 7 are the most obscure in the psalm and describe the fall of the wicked leaders and the scattered state of the faithful. Verses 8 to 10 return to a clear prayer: eyes fixed on God, refuge in Him, and the snares of the wicked turned on themselves.

The poem works with a chiasm of danger. The prayer begins and ends with threats from outside, the company of the wicked in verse 4 and the snares in verses 9 and 10. At the centre are threats from within, the lips and heart. The reader is meant to see that the enemy outside and the weakness inside belong together. The poet asks for protection from the one without asking God to turn a blind eye to the other.

A distinctive device is the contrast of tastes. In verse 4 the poet will not 'feast on their delicacies,' and in verse 6 he says that his words 'are pleasant.' Both words come from the same Hebrew root meaning sweet or pleasant. The pleasures of the wicked and the pleasantness of the word of truth are set side by side, as rival appetites. The psalm ends not with an explosion of anger but with the quiet image of the wicked in their own nets and the poet 'passing by in safety.'
context.historical:
The title is 'A psalm of David,' and the likeliest background is again the period when David was on the run from Saul and surrounded by men who might drag him into compromise or betray him. The psalm's worries are those of a man who has been in the company of the powerful and the violent and knows how easily a person can be pulled along. It has an air of a man in danger who wants more than anything to stay clean.

The psalm's central image is drawn from the sanctuary. The 'evening offering' was part of the daily burnt offering, a lamb offered at twilight with grain and drink offering, Exodus 29:38-41. Alongside it the priest burned incense on the golden altar morning and evening, Exodus 30:7-8. The recipe for the incense was holy and could not be copied for private use, Exodus 30:34-38. David could not himself burn that incense, since he was not a priest, and in exile or in flight he could not come to the sanctuary at all. He therefore asks that his prayer count as the incense and his lifted hands as the evening offering. The ritual is the model, and prayer takes its place.

Lifting the hands was the normal posture of prayer in Israel, as in Psalm 28:2 and Psalm 134:2. The evening sacrifice became in later times a fixed hour of prayer: Elijah prayed at the time of the evening sacrifice, 1 Kings 18:36; Ezra rose from his humiliation at the evening offering and spread out his hands, Ezra 9:5; and Daniel received Gabriel at that hour, Daniel 9:21. In the New Testament Peter and John went up to the temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer, Acts 3:1, and Luke shows the people praying outside while Zechariah burned incense, Luke 1:9-10.

The 'delicacies' of verse 4 belong to the world of court patronage, where a banquet could be a bribe or a bond. Proverbs warns against craving the delicacies of a ruler, Proverbs 23:3, and Daniel refused the king's food, Daniel 1:8. To eat at someone's table was to be tied to him. The psalm's refusal is a refusal to be bought.
context.canonical:
Psalm 141 links the worship of the sanctuary to the prayer of the heart, and the rest of Scripture builds on that link. Psalm 116:17 speaks of a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and Hosea speaks of presenting 'the fruit of our lips,' Hosea 14:2, a thought that Hebrews 13:15 carries forward: 'Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name.' The incense of prayer is taken up in the Revelation, where the golden bowls full of incense 'are the prayers of the saints,' Revelation 5:8, and an angel offers incense with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar, Revelation 8:3-4. What David asked for as a hope is shown as a heavenly fact.

The prayer for a guard on the mouth is echoed in Psalm 39:1, 'I will guard my mouth with a muzzle,' and in Psalm 19:14, 'May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be pleasing in Your sight.' The wisdom books say the same, Proverbs 13:3 and 21:23, and James builds a whole argument on the tongue, James 3:2-8. Jesus says that what comes from the mouth comes from the heart, Matthew 15:18-19, and that people will give account for every careless word, Matthew 12:36. The psalm's pairing of mouth and heart, verses 3 and 4, is the same as His.

The welcome of rebuke belongs to the wisdom tradition. 'Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge,' Proverbs 12:1, 'The wounds of a friend are faithful,' Proverbs 27:6, and the New Testament teaches that the Lord's discipline is a sign of love, Hebrews 12:5-6 and Revelation 3:19. The exhortation to restore a brother gently, Galatians 6:1, gives the other side of the picture: someone must do the rebuking.

Verse 8's eyes fixed on God recall Psalm 123:1-2 and Psalm 25:15, and find their New Testament form in Hebrews 12:2, 'Let us fix our eyes on Jesus.' The picture of the wicked falling into their own nets, verse 10, belongs with Psalm 7:15-16, Psalm 9:15 and Proverbs 26:27, and its companion, Psalm 140, is the closest neighbour.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wanted to teach a prayer that goes to the root. Many prayers ask for escape from the enemy. This one asks first to be kept from becoming like him. The poet knows the danger is not only the trap outside but the pull inside: a word spoken in anger, a heart that drifts, a taste for the pleasures of the powerful. He asks God to set a guard at the door of his lips and to hold his heart back from evil before he says a word about his enemies' fate.

He also meant to honour correction. For a man of his standing, a king or a future king, to say 'Let the righteous man strike me' is remarkable, and it is meant to show Israel that wisdom welcomes rebuke. The sign of a godly person is the willingness to be corrected by the faithful.

A third aim is to bring the temple into the believer's day. Prayer is not a poor substitute for the sanctuary but takes the place of its daily offering, and any Israelite far from Jerusalem could use these words. The poet teaches that God receives sincere prayer as He receives incense.

Lastly, the psalm teaches where to look when under threat. 'My eyes are fixed on You,' verse 8, is the posture of refuge. The first hearers were meant to leave with the sense that safety is not a matter of cunning but of looking in the right direction.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes David's prayer in a particular time of danger, and several of its lines are about circumstances that few readers share, such as rulers thrown from cliffs and bones scattered at the mouth of Sheol. It does not tell believers to expect those events. The final prayer that the wicked fall into their own nets is a request to God, which should not be carried out by the one who prays.

What the psalm prescribes is a way of praying and living. Pray as an offering. Set the hour of prayer within the daily rhythm, as the evening offering did. Ask for a guard on the mouth, for the heart to be kept from evil, and for the company one keeps to be safe. Welcome rebuke from the righteous and treat it as kindness. Keep the eyes on God.

Care is needed with the picture of lifted hands and incense. The text does not require a physical posture, and the New Testament speaks of 'lifting up holy hands' as a sign of a clean heart, 1 Timothy 2:8, not as a ritual. Nor does the psalm require a set hour, though the pattern shows that a regular time can sustain prayer. And the welcome of rebuke does not mean that every critic is a righteous man. The psalm says 'the righteous man,' and it is the character of the one who rebukes that makes the blow a kindness. A believer is also called to give such rebuke in love, Galatians 6:1, and not only to receive it.

debates.question: What is the meaning of verse 5, 'It is oil for my head'?

views.label: The rebuke of the righteous is like precious oil
views.case: The BSB and many translations take the rebuke as the oil: the correction of a faithful man is a gift that honours and refreshes, as the anointing oil honoured a guest, Psalm 23:5. Proverbs 27:6 supports it by saying the wounds of a friend are faithful.

views.label: The wicked's oil is to be refused
views.case: The ancient Greek version reads the verse as a contrast: let the righteous correct me in mercy, but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head. On this reading the oil is the flattery or patronage of the wicked, and it fits the refusal of their delicacies in verse 4.

views.label: A word play with a poisonous plant
views.case: The Hebrew word for head, rosh, is also the name of a bitter, poisonous plant, so some propose that the line speaks of a rebuke that is bitter but healing. This reading is more speculative and has few defenders.

debates.bearing: The first reading yields a clear and usable point and is the one most English versions adopt. The second has strong support in the context of verse 4. Either way, the psalm contrasts what honest rebuke gives with what the company of the wicked offers.

debates.question: What are verses 6 and 7 saying?

views.label: A judgment on the wicked rulers and a lament of the faithful
views.case: The rulers of the wicked are thrown down and the people then listen to the poet's pleasant words, while the faithful describe themselves as scattered like soil broken by the plough. This is the most common reading of the BSB's rendering.

views.label: A picture of the poet's own near-death
views.case: The bones scattered at the mouth of Sheol are the speaker's own, and the verses describe how near death he has come, with the wicked leaders as the ones who brought him there.

views.label: A textually uncertain passage
views.case: The Hebrew of both verses is difficult and translations differ widely, so the wise reader should hold any interpretation loosely and not build a doctrine on them.

debates.bearing: The meaning of the details is uncertain, but the thrust is clear in the verses that follow: whatever the danger, the poet turns his eyes to God in verse 8, and that turn is the point of the passage.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 joins two sanctuary words. The first is ketoret, incense, from the root meaning to make smoke rise, the fragrant blend burned morning and evening on the golden altar, Exodus 30:7-8. The second is minchat arev, the evening offering, where minchah is the grain offering or gift and arev is evening. Together they compare prayer to the two daily moments of the temple. The word for 'uplifted' in 'my uplifted hands' is from the verb nasa, to lift or carry, and the noun made from it, mas'at, means a lifting. The psalm turns the posture into a sacrifice.

In verse 3 the poet prays for a 'guard,' shamrah, to be set over his mouth, and for a 'watch,' natsrah, to be kept at the door of his lips. Both verbs belong to the vocabulary of sentries and watchmen. The same pair of roots, shamar and natsar, is used of God as the keeper of His people, for example in Psalm 121:7, where the LORD guards from all evil. The image is of a gate with a watchman, and the request is that God Himself take the post.

Verse 4 uses 'delicacies' and verse 6 uses 'pleasant,' and both come from a root meaning sweet, agreeable. The poet will not feast on the wicked's sweet things, and at the end he says that his own words, or the words he will speak, are sweet in a better sense. The same root appears for the pleasantness of living together in Psalm 133:1. The psalm is arranging two kinds of sweetness against each other, and the better sweetness comes in the end.

Verse 5 turns on 'loving devotion,' chesed. The BSB renders the line 'let his rebuke be an act of loving devotion.' The poet calls the strike of the righteous man chesed, covenant kindness. The same word that describes God's faithful love to His people describes a rebuke given within the covenant community. That is a bold application, and it lines up with Proverbs 27:6, where the wounds of a friend are 'faithful.' The word 'rebuke' is from the verb yakach, to reprove or set right, the word of Proverbs 9:8 and 25:12.

In verse 8 the poet asks God not to 'leave my soul defenseless.' The BSB footnote says the Hebrew can read 'do not pour out my life' or 'do not give me over to death.' The verb is the one for pouring out or laying bare, and it is used in Isaiah 53:12 of the Servant who 'poured out His life unto death.' In the psalm it is a prayer not to be emptied, and in Isaiah it is the act of the Servant who willingly was. The two uses of the same verb are worth holding side by side, though the psalm does not refer to Isaiah.

Verse 10 speaks of the wicked falling into 'their own nets,' using a word for a net that is not the common resheth, and 'I pass by' uses the verb avar, to cross over, a gentle word for escaping. The picture is of the trapper caught and the hunted going on his way.

typology.type: The prayer set before God like incense, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: The daily incense on the golden altar pointed to prayers rising before God. Luke records the people praying outside while Zechariah burned incense, Luke 1:9-10, and Revelation shows the prayers of the saints as incense in golden bowls and on the golden altar before the throne, Revelation 5:8 and 8:3-4. The escalation is that the prayers are carried through the Lamb and heard in heaven, Hebrews 4:14-16. The type falls short in that incense was burned by priests, whereas now every believer is welcome in the holy place through Christ's blood, Hebrews 10:19-22.

typology.type: The uplifted hands like the evening offering, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: David asks that his hands count as the evening sacrifice. The evening lamb of Exodus 29:41 was part of Israel's daily worship, and the Gospels place the death of Jesus at the ninth hour, Mark 15:34-37 and Luke 23:44-46, the afternoon hour of prayer, Acts 3:1. The link is one of timing and theme and should not be pressed into an exact claim about the temple's schedule. The escalation is that the lamb was Christ Himself, who offered Himself as a fragrant sacrifice, Ephesians 5:2. The type falls short because a lamb was offered daily, but Christ offered Himself once for all, Hebrews 10:10.

typology.type: The guard on the mouth, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: The poet asks for what Jesus lived out. When abused, Christ 'did not retaliate,' and 'made no threats,' 1 Peter 2:23, and before His accusers He kept silent, Isaiah 53:7, and Mark 15:5. His mouth was kept from every careless word, which is the standard against which Matthew 12:36 speaks. The escalation is that the Son did not need a guard, since no deceit was found in His mouth, 1 Peter 2:22, and by His Spirit He changes the speech of His people, Ephesians 4:29. The type falls short because David is asking for help he could not give himself.

typology.type: The righteous man's rebuke received as loving devotion, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: The welcome of rebuke finds an example in Peter, who was opposed to his face by Paul when his conduct was not in step with the gospel, Galatians 2:11-14, and later called Paul 'our beloved brother,' 2 Peter 3:15. The greater example is the Lord who disciplines those He loves, Hebrews 12:5-6, and who says, 'Those I love, I rebuke and discipline,' Revelation 3:19. The escalation is that the final righteous One is Christ, whose word wounds in order to heal. The type has limits: the psalm speaks of human rebukers, who may err, while Christ's rebuke is always right.

study.christ:
Psalm 141 is not applied to Jesus by name in the New Testament, but its main images are either fulfilled in Him or are the habits of life He taught and kept. The reader should treat the links as ones of pattern and fulfilment, not as proof texts.

The first is prayer as an offering. David asks that his prayer be treated as the incense and his lifted hands as the evening sacrifice. In Jesus those pictures meet. He is the Priest through whom believers can approach God. The writer to the Hebrews says that Christ holds His priesthood permanently, and that He 'always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:24-25. Revelation shows the prayers of the saints rising with incense from the altar before the throne, Revelation 8:3-4. The believer's prayer reaches God not on its own merit but because of the Mediator, and Hebrews 13:15 says 'through Jesus' we offer the sacrifice of praise.

The second is the sacrifice itself. The evening offering was a lamb, and John the Baptist pointed to Jesus as 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' John 1:29. He died at the ninth hour, Mark 15:34-37, with His hands stretched out in a way the psalm could not have foreseen. The link is not a precise prediction but it is a fitting rhyme: the lifted hands of the psalmist and the stretched hands of Christ on the cross are both offered to the Father, and the second is the one that gives the first its meaning.

The third is the guarded mouth. Jesus is the one in whose mouth no deceit was found, 1 Peter 2:22. His silence before Pilate and Herod fulfils Isaiah 53:7. His 'Father, forgive them,' Luke 23:34, is the speech of a guarded mouth when it was most provoked. In the Garden He told His disciples to 'Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation,' Matthew 26:41, and taught them to pray, 'lead us not into temptation,' Matthew 6:13, the same prayer as verse 4: do not let my heart be drawn to evil.

The fourth is the eyes fixed on God. 'My eyes are fixed on You' becomes in Hebrews 12:2 the posture of faith toward Jesus, who 'for the joy set before Him endured the cross.' He is both the One who kept His eyes on the Father and the One on whom the believer's eyes are fixed. The psalm's last request, that the wicked fall into their own nets while the faithful pass by in safety, finds a pattern in the cross, where the powers thought they had trapped Him and were disarmed, Colossians 2:15.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The details of verses 5 to 7 are uncertain, and the psalm should not be treated as a coded forecast of the passion. What it offers is a way of praying that Jesus perfected, and the assurance that the prayer reaches God through Him.
study.god:
Psalm 141 shows God as the one who hears, who guards, who corrects, and who is the refuge of those who look to Him.

God hears prayer as an offering. The comparison to incense and the evening sacrifice says that He receives the prayer of a sincere person as He received the gifts at His altar, and that His attention to a single voice is a matter of delight. 'Come quickly to me,' verse 1, shows the believer's confidence in a God who can come, and 'Hear my voice' shows the assumption that He does. The Psalter elsewhere calls Him 'O You who listen to prayer,' Psalm 65:2.

God is a keeper. The prayer 'Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth' presumes that He is able to watch the doors of a person's inner life, which are places no human sentry can reach. The same God is addressed as 'the LORD your keeper,' Psalm 121:5. To the human instinct that the greatest danger is outside, the psalm adds that the heart and tongue need God's watch more than the walls need a gate. This is a God who is concerned with the formation of a person, not merely their protection.

God is the author of correction. To ask for the rebuke of the righteous is to trust that God works through faithful people to turn a person from error. The Lord disciplines those He loves, Hebrews 12:6, and the psalm calls even a blow chesed. It shows a God whose love is not soft.

God is the sovereign over the wicked. The nets they lay and the plots they devise are within His hand, and He can let them be caught in their own devices. He is not mocked. The prayer of verse 10 does not ask God to do something strange; it asks Him to let the moral order of the world work, as Proverbs 26:27 says it will.

God is the refuge of the defenceless. 'In You I seek refuge,' verse 8, is the same confession as Psalm 34:22: none who take refuge in Him will be condemned. The psalm sees no contradiction between a God of power and a God who gives shelter to a small person.

For worship the psalm teaches honesty about the divided human heart, the willingness to be corrected, and a steady gaze on God. It also shows that prayer at the end of the day, when hands are lifted and the day's work is over, is a form of offering that God receives with pleasure.

crossReferences.note: The daily burnt offering consisted of a lamb in the morning and a lamb at twilight, with grain and drink offerings, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. It is the ritual behind 'the evening offering' in Psalm 141:2, and it shows that David asks for his prayer to take the place of Israel's daily sacrifice.

Aaron was to burn fragrant incense on the altar every morning and at twilight, perpetually before the LORD. It is the other half of the picture in Psalm 141:2: prayer as incense. The commandment shows that this was a daily, unbroken offering, which the psalm applies to prayer.

An angel offers incense with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne, and the smoke rises before God. It is the heavenly fulfilment of Psalm 141:2, where David could only hope that his prayer would rise like incense.

David resolves to guard his mouth with a muzzle while the wicked are present. It is the human side of the prayer in Psalm 141:3: there he asks God to set the guard, here he promises to set it himself. Together they show effort and dependence belonging together.

The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful. It gives the principle behind Psalm 141:5: the strike of a righteous man is a kindness, while the smooth words and delicacies of the wicked are a danger.

Do not crave the ruler's delicacies, for that food is deceptive. It matches the refusal of Psalm 141:4 to feast on the wicked's delicacies, and shows how a rich table can be a snare. The psalm and the proverb agree that pleasure offered by the wrongdoer has a price.

The proud hide a snare and spread a net. Psalm 141:9 uses two of the same words for the traps laid for the poet, so the two psalms read as a pair of prayers against the same danger, one for rescue and one for keeping a clean heart.

The wicked man digs a pit and falls into it, and his violence returns on his own head. It states the principle behind Psalm 141:10, that the wicked fall into their own nets, and it gives the prayer its footing in the moral order of God's world.

Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross. It gives the Christian form of Psalm 141:8, 'My eyes are fixed on You,' and names the One on whom the believer's eyes now rest.

Through Jesus let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name. It applies the picture of Psalm 141:2 to the church: prayer and praise are the offering, and Christ is the way through which it goes up.

What comes out of the mouth comes from the heart, and defiles a person. It links the mouth and heart as Psalm 141:3-4 does, and shows that Jesus shared the psalm's insight that guarding the lips is the same task as guarding the heart.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 141 begins with an offering and ends with a trap sprung on the trappers, and its place in the Bible's story is on the line between worship and temptation. In the garden, a mouth and a hand did the first harm: the woman took and ate, Genesis 3:6, and the man spoke to blame, Genesis 3:12. The psalm prays for a mouth and a hand that act in a different way. The poet asks that his lips be guarded, that his heart not be drawn to evil, and that he not feast on what the wicked offer, which is a deliberate reversal of the first meal.

The psalm also takes its place in the story of how God provides for approach. Israel was given a tabernacle, a priesthood, an altar, and a daily offering at morning and evening. Those arrangements told the people that sinners can draw near, but only by a way God provides. David, away from the sanctuary, asks that prayer be received as the offering, and Hosea speaks of presenting the fruit of the lips, Hosea 14:2. The temple would be destroyed and the exiles would pray without it, as Daniel did, but the offering of prayer continued, Daniel 6:10 and 9:21.

In Christ the arrangement is completed. The Lamb was offered once, and His priesthood is permanent, so that those who come to God through Him are heard, Hebrews 7:25. The church now offers 'a sacrifice of praise,' Hebrews 13:15, and the incense of its prayers rises in heaven, Revelation 8:3-4. The Spirit, who is given to those who believe, helps them in their weakness and guards their hearts, Romans 8:26, which is the answer to the psalm's most inward request.

The story ends with a people whose mouths are clean. In the new creation 'no lie was found in their mouths,' Revelation 14:5, and the nets of the wicked are gone, and the evening offering is no longer needed because the Lamb Himself is the light of the city, Revelation 21:23. The poet who asked for a guard at the door of his lips is answered by a people who see God's face, and who no longer need to be guarded from themselves. What began as a prayer at twilight is fulfilled in a day that has no night, Revelation 22:5.

sermon.title: Pray for God to Meet You
sermon.why: In this Look at the Book study on Psalm 141:1-4, Piper explores why David prays for God to come, unpacking the psalm's opening plea and its call to guard the mouth, directly serving this passage's structure and themes.

quiz.q: What does David ask concerning his prayer in verse 2?

options.text: That it be set before God like incense, and his lifted hands like the evening offering.
options.note: David borrows temple worship language to frame his prayer as an acceptable offering to God.

options.text: That it be answered only after a long delay for testing.
options.note: The verse asks that prayer be received like a worship offering, not that it be delayed.

options.text: That it be judged according to how eloquent his words are.
options.note: The request is about acceptance as worship, not eloquence of speech.

options.text: That it never be heard by anyone but himself.
options.note: The prayer is directed openly to God as an offering, not hidden from being heard.

quiz.q: What does David ask God to guard in verse 3?

options.text: His mouth, asking the LORD to keep watch at the door of his lips.
options.note: This is the psalm's central request, guarding speech from evil words.

options.text: His house from physical intruders.
options.note: The request concerns his mouth and speech, not his physical dwelling.

options.text: His wealth from being stolen.
options.note: The psalm is not concerned with material possessions here but with guarded speech.

options.text: His army from defeat in battle.
options.note: The request is personal and inward, guarding his mouth, not a request about military forces.

quiz.q: How does David describe the rebuke of a righteous person in verse 5?

options.text: As an act of loving devotion and like oil for his head, something he should not refuse.
options.note: David frames godly correction as a healing kindness rather than an insult to be resisted.

options.text: As a betrayal he must avenge.
options.note: The verse frames rebuke as kindness to welcome, not betrayal to avenge.

options.text: As something to be politely ignored.
options.note: David explicitly says let me not refuse it, welcoming rather than ignoring the correction.

options.text: As proof that the righteous person is actually his enemy.
options.note: The verse specifically calls this rebuke an act of loving devotion, not evidence of enmity.

quiz.q: Where does David say his eyes are fixed in verse 8?

options.text: On God the Lord, in whom he seeks refuge.
options.note: This declaration anchors the psalm's closing confidence in God alone as refuge.

options.text: On his own military strength and strategy.
options.note: David turns his gaze to God, not to self-reliance or strategy.

options.text: On the wealth of his enemies.
options.note: The verse is about trust in God, not envy of enemies' possessions.

options.text: On escaping to a foreign nation for safety.
options.note: David seeks refuge in God directly, not in fleeing to another nation.

quiz.q: What does David expect will happen to the wicked in verse 10?

options.text: That they will fall into their own nets while he passes by safely.
options.note: This reversal, the trapper caught in his own trap, closes the psalm with confident trust in God's justice.

options.text: That they will escape all consequences permanently.
options.note: The verse expects the opposite, that the wicked will fall into the very traps they set.

options.text: That David himself must personally destroy them.
options.note: David entrusts their downfall to their own schemes and to God, not to his own hand.

options.text: That he will join them in their schemes to survive.
options.note: The whole psalm has asked God to keep David from joining in the wicked's schemes, verse 4, not to join them.

questions: David asks that his prayer be received like incense, a fragrant, acceptable offering to God. What would it look like for your prayer life this week to feel less like a duty and more like worship offered to God?
David prays first for a guarded mouth and heart before praying for rescue from his enemies. Where do you most need God to set a guard over your mouth or heart right now?

David welcomes a righteous friend's rebuke as an act of loving devotion, oil for his head. How do you typically respond to correction, and what would it take to receive it as a kindness rather than an attack?
David refuses to feast on the delicacies of those who do wickedness, even while surrounded by danger. What compromises are you being tempted toward for the sake of comfort or safety?

David fixes his eyes on God alone as refuge rather than on his own strength or strategy. What would it mean this week to fix your eyes on God rather than on your own attempts to manage a difficult situation?

translationNotes.note: The evening offering refers to the daily evening sacrifice at the temple, Exodus 29:39, which David's prayer is likened to even though he may have been far from the sanctuary at the time.

When their rulers are thrown down from the cliffs pictures a scene of decisive judgment on those who oppose God, after which David's own words will be recognized by the people as trustworthy and welcome.
Do not leave my soul defenseless carries an alternate rendering, do not pour out my life, both readings expressing David's plea that God not abandon him to his enemies' traps.
